questions.stem: A 74 year old man with schizophrenia treated with clozapine has a 3 day history of increasing abdominal distension and pain. He has not opened his bowels or passed flatus for 2 days. His abdomen is grossly distended and tympanic. An abdominal X-ray shows a massively dilated inverted U-shaped loop of colon arising from the pelvis, with a central dividing line.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A massively dilated inverted U loop from the pelvis with a central line is the coffee bean sign of sigmoid volvulus; clozapine-induced constipation is the predisposing factor.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: inverted U-shaped loop of colon arising from the pelvis
steps.x: Chronic constipation plus a giant twisted pelvic loop is the coffee bean sign.

elim: Gives a comma-shaped loop from the right lower quadrant (embryo sign) with small bowel dilatation.
Diffuse colonic dilatation without a twisted loop or coffee bean shape.
Central dilated loops with valvulae conniventes, not a giant pelvic colonic loop.
Follows severe colitis with bloody diarrhoea and systemic toxicity.

steps.x: Coffee bean sign on AXR = sigmoid volvulus, the commonest volvulus in adults.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has a 1 day history of colicky abdominal pain and repeated vomiting. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. He is tender in the right iliac fossa. An abdominal X-ray shows a large comma-shaped dilated loop of bowel arising from the right lower quadrant and lying in the left upper abdomen, with dilated small bowel loops.

visual.title: Where the pain is
visual.caption: Right iliac fossa tenderness with a small bowel obstruction picture points to the caecum.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A comma-shaped loop arising from the right lower quadrant (embryo sign), RIF tenderness and a small bowel obstruction picture are caecal volvulus.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: tender in the right iliac fossa
arising from the right lower quadrant
steps.x: RIF tenderness, vomiting and an SBO picture with a comma-shaped loop from the right: caecal.

elim: RIF pain with fever, but no giant dilated loop or obstruction on X-ray.
Gives subacute obstruction with weight loss and diarrhoea, not a giant twisted loop.
Commonest in infants; in adults gives a target sign on CT, not an embryo sign.
Gives a coffee bean loop arising from the pelvis with large bowel obstruction.

steps.x: Embryo sign = caecal volvulus: RIF tenderness and a small bowel obstruction-type picture.

questions.stem: An 87 year old woman in a nursing home has a 2 day history of abdominal swelling, nausea and absolute constipation. She has long-standing constipation and is largely bedbound. Her abdomen is massively distended and tympanic with tinkling bowel sounds. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal X-ray?
questions.e: A bedbound, constipated nursing home resident with large bowel obstruction has sigmoid volvulus, which shows a coffee bean sign on abdominal X-ray.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely finding on abdominal X-ray?
Elderly, institutionalised, constipated, with LBO: sigmoid volvulus until proven otherwise.

elim: Duodenal atresia in neonates.
Caecal volvulus, which gives an SBO-type picture with RIF tenderness.
Free intraperitoneal gas after perforation; she has no peritonism.
Bowel wall oedema in ischaemic or infective colitis.

steps.x: Sigmoid volvulus on AXR: coffee bean sign, a twisted dilated sigmoid loop.

questions.stem: A 92 year old man with advanced dementia in a care home has not passed stool or flatus for 3 days. He has vomited twice. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. An abdominal X-ray later shows a coffee bean sign. His potassium is 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.3).
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
o: Board-like rigidity with absent bowel sounds
Tender mass in the right iliac fossa
Tympanic distension with tinkling bowel sounds
questions.e: Uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus gives a large bowel obstruction picture: massive tympanic distension, tinkling bowel sounds, constipation and vomiting.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?

clues: not passed stool or flatus for 3 days
steps.x: Coffee bean means sigmoid volvulus; he is stable, so expect an obstructed, gas-filled abdomen, not peritonism.

elim: Suggests perforation and peritonitis; he is afebrile and stable.
Suggests an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Indicates ascites; a gas-filled loop is resonant.
Suggests an appendix mass or caecal tumour.

steps.x: Sigmoid volvulus examination: tympanic distension and tinkling (obstructed) bowel sounds.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has a 12 hour history of abdominal pain. A CT is planned to decide whether she has a caecal or sigmoid volvulus. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 126/76 mmHg. She has had no previous constipation.
questions.q: Which clinical feature would most suggest caecal rather than sigmoid volvulus?
o: Age over 80 and nursing home residence
Early vomiting with right iliac fossa tenderness
Massive distension rising out of the pelvis
questions.e: Caecal volvulus behaves like small bowel obstruction with early vomiting and right iliac fossa tenderness; sigmoid volvulus gives a large bowel obstruction picture.

steps.x: The question asks: which clinical feature would most suggest caecal rather than sigmoid volvulus?
Separate the two by obstruction level: caecal = SBO-type (vomit early, RIF); sigmoid = LBO-type (distension, constipation).

elim: Typical of the large bowel obstruction picture of sigmoid volvulus.
Risk factors for sigmoid volvulus.
Chronic constipation predisposes to sigmoid volvulus.
The giant sigmoid loop of sigmoid volvulus.

steps.x: Caecal volvulus: RIF tenderness and SBO picture. Sigmoid: LBO picture.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man has sigmoid volvulus that has been decompressed. He lives alone, walks very little and takes codeine for osteoarthritis. He has needed laxatives for many years. He asks what made his bowel twist.
questions.q: Which is the most likely predisposing factor?
questions.e: Chronic constipation (here from opioids and immobility) produces an elongated, redundant sigmoid that is mobile enough to twist.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely predisposing factor?
Opioids plus immobility in an old man means chronic constipation and a redundant sigmoid.

elim: Causes malabsorption and diarrhoea, not a redundant sigmoid.
Affects the stomach and oesophageal junction, not the sigmoid colon.
Protects against constipation.
Adhesions cause small bowel obstruction, not sigmoid volvulus.

steps.x: Risk factors: elderly, nursing home, chronic constipation, congenital malformation: all give a redundant, mobile loop.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman has sigmoid volvulus on abdominal X-ray. The registrar explains to a student that the twisted loop is blocked at both its entry and exit points, so gas cannot escape upwards or downwards. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely type of obstruction she has?
questions.e: Volvulus obstructs both ends of the twisted segment, a closed-loop obstruction, which raises intraluminal pressure quickly.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely type of obstruction she has?

clues: blocked at both its entry and exit points
steps.x: Both ends blocked = closed loop.

elim: A functional obstruction without a mechanical twist.
A functional dilatation without a mechanical cause.
Only one end is blocked; gas can decompress backwards.
Some flatus passes and the colon is not twisted.

steps.x: Volvulus = closed-loop obstruction: both ends of the segment obstructed.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman had abdominal distension at home for 4 days before admission. An abdominal X-ray shows a coffee bean sign. She now has constant severe pain. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 96/58 mmHg. Her lower abdomen is rigid with rebound tenderness. Venous lactate is 5.8 mmol/L (0.5–2.0).
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
o: Ischaemic necrosis of the twisted sigmoid loop
questions.e: A delayed presentation with constant pain, fever, peritonism and a raised lactate means the twisted loop has become ischaemic and may perforate.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely complication?
Constant pain, peritonism and high lactate in volvulus: ischaemia, with perforation next.

elim: Dilatation without a twist; it does not explain peritonism and a high lactate.
Gives LIF tenderness and fever but not a coffee bean loop.
Gives painless distension without rigidity or high lactate.
Would relieve distension and pain, not cause peritonism.

steps.x: Volvulus complications: closed loop, then ischaemia and perforation, then sepsis.

questions.stem: A 90 year old man from a care home is admitted confused and drowsy. His carers report 3 days of a swollen abdomen and no bowel movement. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 86/50 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. His abdomen is distended and tender. Urine dipstick is negative. An abdominal X-ray shows a coffee bean sign.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Colonic pseudo-obstruction with a urinary infection
questions.e: A coffee bean loop with fever, tachycardia, hypotension and confusion is sigmoid volvulus with sepsis, usually from ischaemic or perforated bowel.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?
The source is the twisted bowel: shock plus coffee bean, with no urinary source.

elim: Gives profuse diarrhoea, not absolute constipation with a coffee bean loop.
The coffee bean sign shows a mechanical twist, and the urine is clear.
Causes constipation and overflow diarrhoea but not a twisted loop or shock.
He is febrile, hypotensive and confused, so this is not uncomplicated.

steps.x: Volvulus can cause ischaemia, perforation and sepsis; shock means complicated volvulus.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman is 4 days after a hip hemiarthroplasty. She has developed abdominal distension and has not passed flatus. A colleague suspects acute colonic pseudo-obstruction. Her abdomen is distended and tympanic but not tender. An abdominal X-ray shows a single massively dilated inverted U-shaped sigmoid loop with its apex under the left hemidiaphragm and a central dividing line.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: The coffee bean sign (a single dilated inverted U sigmoid loop with a central line) is sigmoid volvulus, a mechanical twist, even in a post-operative patient where pseudo-obstruction is common.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: single massively dilated inverted U-shaped sigmoid loop
steps.x: The X-ray shape wins over the setting: a single twisted loop is volvulus, not pseudo-obstruction.

elim: Classic after hip surgery, but gives diffuse colonic dilatation, not a single twisted loop.
The loop arises from the right lower quadrant (embryo sign).
Gives diffuse gas in small and large bowel without a twisted loop.
Gives central loops with valvulae conniventes.

steps.x: Coffee bean sign = sigmoid volvulus, a mechanical closed loop, not pseudo-obstruction.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has abdominal distension and absolute constipation for 2 days. An abdominal X-ray shows dilated large bowel but is not diagnostic. A CT abdomen shows a dilated sigmoid colon with a 'whirl' of mesentery and vessels twisted around a point in the left lower abdomen, with two adjacent points of narrowing.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: CT characterises volvulus when the X-ray is unclear: a mesenteric whirl with two adjacent narrowing points shows the sigmoid has twisted around its mesentery.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?
A twist of mesentery around a point with two narrowings is a closed-loop twist; left-sided means sigmoid.

elim: The twist would be in the right lower quadrant with a dilated caecum.
No mechanical transition point or mesenteric twist.
Gives a single shouldered mass at the transition point, not a mesenteric whirl.
Gives fat stranding and thickened wall with diverticula, not a twist.

steps.x: Volvulus = twisting of bowel around its mesentery; CT is second-line when AXR is inconclusive.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with a learning disability who lives in residential care has a 2 day history of abdominal distension. He takes hyoscine for drooling and has had constipation for years. His abdomen is grossly distended and tympanic. He has not passed flatus. His temperature is 37.0°C and pulse rate 98 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Institutionalised patients with chronic constipation (here from anticholinergics) develop a redundant sigmoid that twists, giving a large bowel obstruction picture.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?
Not only the elderly: any institutionalised, chronically constipated patient is at risk.

elim: Gives an SBO-type picture with early vomiting and RIF tenderness, without long-standing constipation.
Presents in infancy with delayed passage of meconium.
Gives bloating and altered habit but not absolute constipation with gross tympany.
Needs previous surgery and gives early vomiting with central distension.

steps.x: Sigmoid volvulus risk: institutionalised, chronic constipation, elderly; LBO picture.

questions.stem: A 90 year old man with a previous stroke lives in a nursing home. He has a 2 day history of abdominal distension and has not opened his bowels. His abdomen is tympanic and mildly tender with no guarding. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Suspected sigmoid volvulus is confirmed with an abdominal X-ray showing the coffee bean sign.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

clues: abdominal distension and has not opened his bowels
steps.x: Elderly, institutionalised, LBO picture: get an AXR to look for the coffee bean sign.

elim: Gas-filled bowel makes ultrasound unhelpful in obstruction.
Not a first-line test; contrast studies are not used acutely.
Not the first investigation and insufflation risks perforation.
Slow and not used for acute bowel obstruction.

steps.x: Volvulus: AXR confirms (coffee bean or embryo sign); CT if inconclusive.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman has sigmoid volvulus confirmed on abdominal X-ray. Before attempting decompression, the surgeon is worried about ischaemia because she has a temperature of 38.0°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and localised tenderness over the distended loop. Her BP is 124/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate further imaging investigation?
o: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
questions.e: CT abdomen is the second-line test that further characterises volvulus, including signs of ischaemia or perforation, before choosing decompression or surgery.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate further imaging investigation?
The question is the state of the bowel wall; CT shows that, AXR does not.

elim: Contraindicated if bowel may be ischaemic or perforated.
Shows free air but cannot assess bowel wall perfusion.
Invasive and used for arterial mesenteric ischaemia, not volvulus.
Delays recognising ischaemic bowel.

steps.x: CT abdomen characterises volvulus further and looks for ischaemia or perforation.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has a 1 day history of colicky central abdominal pain and vomiting. She had a similar milder episode 6 months ago that settled on its own. Her pulse rate is 102 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. She has right iliac fossa tenderness and a distended upper abdomen. Her pregnancy test is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent colicky pain with RIF tenderness and an SBO picture in a young woman suggests caecal volvulus; an abdominal X-ray shows the embryo sign.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm the most likely diagnosis?
Intermittent twisting of a mobile caecum; the first confirmatory test is AXR (embryo sign).

elim: Not used to diagnose caecal volvulus and risks perforation.
Used for adhesional obstruction, not first-line here.
Assesses ovarian pathology, not a twisted caecum.
Assesses the stomach and duodenum.

steps.x: Caecal volvulus: AXR embryo sign first; CT to characterise.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has caecal volvulus on CT. He is being assessed for theatre. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. The team wants a quick bedside test to show whether the bowel is already compromised.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate bedside investigation?
questions.e: Metabolic acidosis and a high lactate indicate bowel compromise in caecal volvulus and are indications for emergency laparotomy.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate bedside investigation?

clues: whether the bowel is already compromised
steps.x: Ischaemic bowel switches to anaerobic metabolism: acidosis and lactate.

elim: Does not reflect bowel perfusion.
A marker of inflammatory bowel disease, not acute ischaemia.
Mainly used for pancreatitis; not a measure of bowel compromise.
Looks for urinary infection, not ischaemia.

steps.x: Caecal volvulus: acidosis or high lactate = bowel compromise = emergency laparotomy.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has caecal volvulus on CT. The radiologist reports several measurements. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Venous pH is 7.38 and lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Her abdomen is distended but not peritonitic.
questions.q: Which CT finding would most indicate the need for emergency laparotomy?
o: Air-fluid levels in the small bowel
questions.e: A caecum over 12 cm in diameter signals impending perforation and needs emergency laparotomy with ileocaecal resection.

steps.x: The question asks: which CT finding would most indicate the need for emergency laparotomy?
Her bloods show no compromise, so the deciding CT number is the caecal diameter.

elim: Expected in caecal volvulus; does not alone mean impending perforation.
Expected distal to the twist.
Incidental and unrelated.
Mild small bowel dilatation is expected in caecal volvulus.

steps.x: Caecum >12 cm = impending perforation = emergency laparotomy.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with multiple sclerosis and chronic constipation has sigmoid volvulus on abdominal X-ray. He has received IV fluids. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. His abdomen is distended and tympanic but not tender. His lactate is 1.2 mmol/L (0.5–2.0).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Oral macrogol and review in 48 hours
Rigid sigmoidoscopy with insertion of a rectal flatus tube
questions.e: Uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus is treated with immediate decompression by rigid sigmoidoscopy and a rectal flatus tube.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial management?
No peritonism, normal lactate: uncomplicated, so decompress endoscopically.

elim: Barium has no role and risks barium peritonitis.
Reserved for peritonitis, ischaemia or failed decompression.
Laxatives do not untwist a volvulus and delay risks ischaemia.
The operation for caecal volvulus.

steps.x: Uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus: rigid sigmoidoscopy decompression + flatus tube.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman has just had successful rigid sigmoidoscopic decompression of a sigmoid volvulus, with a large release of gas and liquid stool. Her abdomen is now soft and much less distended. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Leave a rectal flatus tube in place
questions.e: After rigid sigmoidoscopic decompression a rectal flatus tube is left in place to keep the loop decompressed and reduce early recurrence.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Decompression worked; keep it decompressed.

elim: Early recurrence is common; she needs a flatus tube and observation.
Not needed after successful decompression without ischaemia.
Slowing the bowel worsens constipation.
The operation for caecal volvulus.

steps.x: Rigid sigmoidoscopy decompression is followed by a rectal flatus tube.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has caecal volvulus with an embryo sign on abdominal X-ray, confirmed on CT. His caecum measures 8 cm. He is not peritonitic. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 130/84 mmHg. Venous lactate is 1.6 mmol/L (0.5–2.0).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Right hemicolectomy with primary ileocolic anastomosis
questions.e: Caecal volvulus is treated surgically with right hemicolectomy and primary ileocolic anastomosis, unlike sigmoid volvulus which is decompressed first.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate definitive management?
Caecal volvulus: no endoscopic fix; it needs resection.

elim: Decompression is rarely successful in caecal volvulus and does not prevent recurrence.
A sigmoid resection with end colostomy.
Second-line for sigmoid volvulus after failed sigmoidoscopy.
First-line for sigmoid volvulus; it cannot reach the caecum.

steps.x: Caecal volvulus first-line: right hemicolectomy with primary ileocolic anastomosis.

questions.stem: A 91 year old woman with severe COPD on home oxygen has sigmoid volvulus. Rigid sigmoidoscopy and flatus tube insertion have failed to decompress the loop. Her abdomen is distended but not tender. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg. The anaesthetist considers her unfit for a general anaesthetic.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Oral laxatives and review in 1 week
questions.e: If sigmoidoscopic decompression fails, percutaneous colostomy tube decompression is the second-line option, especially in a patient unfit for surgery.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate next step in management?
Failed first-line, unfit for surgery, no ischaemia: second-line percutaneous decompression.

elim: Surgical resection is not possible as she is unfit for anaesthesia.
Leaves the closed loop at risk of ischaemia.
Treats caecal volvulus.
Does nothing for the twisted loop.

steps.x: Failed sigmoidoscopic decompression: percutaneous colostomy tube.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man is admitted with his third episode of sigmoid volvulus in 18 months. Each time it was decompressed by rigid sigmoidoscopy. He is otherwise fit and active. His abdomen is now soft after decompression. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
questions.e: Recurrent sigmoid volvulus in a fit patient is managed by surgical resection or fixation of the redundant sigmoid.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate long-term management?
Recurrence + fit for surgery = remove the redundant loop.

elim: Not a long-term solution and does not prevent twisting.
Does not prevent recurrence.
Treats caecal volvulus.
Worsens constipation, which predisposes to volvulus.

steps.x: Sigmoid volvulus failing decompression or recurring: surgical resection/fixation.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has caecal volvulus on CT, with a caecal diameter of 13 cm. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. Venous pH is 7.29 (7.35–7.45) and lactate 4.6 mmol/L (0.5–2.0). She has received IV fluids and antibiotics.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A caecum over 12 cm (impending perforation) and a metabolic acidosis with high lactate (bowel compromise) need emergency laparotomy and ileocaecal resection.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate management?
Two red flags: diameter over 12 cm and acidosis with lactate. Operate now.

elim: Unreliable in caecal volvulus and dangerous with a caecum over 12 cm.
The bowel is already compromised; delay risks perforation.
A second-line option for sigmoid volvulus.
Cannot reach the caecum.

steps.x: Caecal volvulus emergency laparotomy if caecum >12 cm or acidosis/high lactate.

questions.stem: An 85 year old man has sigmoid volvulus. At rigid sigmoidoscopy the mucosa at the twist is black and dusky, and blood-stained fluid is released. Afterwards he has constant pain and lower abdominal guarding. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 108/64 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Leave a rectal flatus tube and observe
questions.e: Necrotic mucosa, peritonism and fever mean ischaemic bowel; sigmoid volvulus with peritonism needs urgent midline laparotomy and resection.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Dead mucosa seen at endoscopy plus peritonism: no more endoscopic attempts.

elim: Appropriate after successful decompression of viable bowel, not with necrotic mucosa.
Does not remove gangrenous bowel.
Delays surgery for necrotic bowel.
The operation for caecal volvulus, not the sigmoid.

steps.x: Volvulus with severe pain, peritonitis or fever: urgent midline laparotomy.

questions.stem: An 83 year old woman has sigmoid volvulus on abdominal X-ray. She has vomited several times. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg and capillary refill time 4 seconds. Her abdomen is distended but not peritonitic. Investigations are shown below. Rigid sigmoidoscopy is planned within the hour.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Nil by mouth, IV fluids and electrolyte replacement
questions.e: Volvulus causes vomiting, third-space loss and electrolyte abnormalities, so she needs NBM, IV fluids and correction of potassium alongside decompression.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate immediate management?
Dry and hypokalaemic from vomiting and obstruction: resuscitate while decompression is arranged.

elim: She is vomiting and obstructed; oral treatment will not be absorbed.
Laxatives do not untwist a volvulus.
Does not decompress a closed loop and can worsen electrolytes.
She has no peritonism; decompression comes first.

steps.x: Volvulus: severe distension, vomiting, electrolyte abnormalities. Resuscitate, then decompress.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has sigmoid volvulus. At a later elective operation, the surgeon shows students the colon. The sigmoid is very long and floppy, and its mesentery is long but attached to the posterior abdominal wall by only a narrow base.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason this anatomy predisposes to volvulus?
o: A long mobile loop can rotate on its narrow mesenteric base
A narrow mesentery increases blood flow to the loop
Diverticula make the colon wall rigid
questions.e: A redundant, mobile sigmoid with a long mesentery and narrow mesenteric attachment can twist on its axis, causing obstruction and, if blood supply is compromised, ischaemia.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely reason this anatomy predisposes to volvulus?
Long loop plus narrow base = something to twist and a pivot to twist around.

elim: A narrow base does not increase blood flow; it creates a pivot point.
Rigidity would resist twisting.
The fixed colon is protected; the problem is mobility.
Describes stricture, not twisting.

steps.x: Volvulus pathophysiology: mobile segment, long mesentery, narrow base, twists on its axis.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has sigmoid volvulus that has been twisted for 2 days. At laparotomy the loop is twisted 360 degrees around its mesentery and the bowel wall is dark purple. The mesenteric veins in the twist are engorged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the bowel ischaemia?
o: Atherosclerotic occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery
Torsion of the mesentery compressing the mesenteric vessels
questions.e: Twisting of the bowel around its mesentery causes luminal obstruction and compresses the mesenteric vessels (veins first, then arteries), leading to ischaemia.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely mechanism of the bowel ischaemia?

clues: mesenteric veins in the twist are engorged
steps.x: The vessels run in the mesentery, which is twisted; venous outflow blocks first.

elim: Chronic mesenteric ischaemia, not volvulus.
Causes acute mesenteric ischaemia without a twist.
Non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia, not a twist.
Inflammatory vessel disease, not mechanical torsion.

steps.x: Volvulus: twist causes obstruction and, if mesenteric supply is compromised, ischaemia.

questions.stem: Two patients are on a surgical ward. One has adhesional small bowel obstruction for 3 days without ischaemia. The other has sigmoid volvulus for 18 hours and already has a raised lactate and peritonism. A student asks why the volvulus has become ischaemic so much faster.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Intraluminal pressure in a closed loop rises rapidly and compromises blood supply
Large bowel has no mesenteric blood supply
Sigmoid volvulus is caused by an arterial embolus
questions.e: In a closed loop both ends are obstructed, so pressure rises quickly, compromising blood flow sooner than in open-loop obstruction and raising the risk of ischaemia and perforation.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely explanation?

clues: adhesional small bowel obstruction for 3 days without ischaemia
steps.x: Compare open loop (can decompress backwards) with closed loop (cannot).

elim: It contains more bacteria, and this does not explain faster ischaemia.
The sigmoid is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery through its mesentery.
Open loops can decompress proximally, so pressure rises more slowly.
Volvulus is a mechanical twist, not an embolus.

steps.x: Closed-loop obstruction: rapid pressure rise, early ischaemia and perforation.

questions.stem: An 80 year old man's abdominal X-ray shows a hugely dilated loop of colon shaped like a coffee bean, rising from the pelvis towards the right upper quadrant. A dense white line runs down the centre of the loop towards the pelvis. A student asks what the central line represents.
questions.q: Which structure most likely forms the central line?
o: The apposed walls of the twisted loop along its mesenteric fold
questions.e: The coffee bean sign is a dilated twisted sigmoid loop whose two limbs meet in the middle; their apposed walls along the mesenteric fold form the central dividing line.

steps.x: The question asks: which structure most likely forms the central line?

clues: dense white line runs down the centre
steps.x: Two dilated limbs of one twisted loop pressed together form the cleft of the bean.

elim: Calcified aorta lies over the spine and is curvilinear, not inside a gas loop.
No contrast has been given.
Lies beside the spine, outside the bowel.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has her second episode of caecal volvulus. Her preoperative X-ray showed a comma-shaped dilated loop in the left upper abdomen.

questions.e: Congenital malformation (failure of the caecum and ascending colon to fix) gives a mobile caecum that twists; the dilated caecum gives the comma-shaped embryo sign.
